claims.claim: Zach Howard judges the introduction to the Holmes Basic Sample Dungeon highly evocative, reading almost like weird fiction.
claims.source: Zach Howard (Zenopus Archives), 'Part 46: "Zenopus Built a Tower"', 2015
claims.quote: The introduction is highly evocative, reading almost like the weird fiction

claims.claim: J. Eric Holmes instructs the Dungeon Master to read the sample dungeon's background material aloud to the assembled players.
claims.source: J. Eric Holmes, D&D Basic Set (1977), quoted by Zach Howard (Zenopus Archives) 2015
claims.quote: should read the background material above to the assembled players

claims.claim: Howard reads Holmes's Portown background as material meant to be read to the players, predating boxed text.
claims.source: Zach Howard (Zenopus Archives), 'Part 46', 2015
claims.quote: this background material is meant to be read to the players

claims.claim: Howard calls Holmes's one-paragraph account of Portown's trade, ships and inhabitants a thumbnail sketch of a campaign setting.
claims.source: Zach Howard (Zenopus Archives), 'Part 46', 2015
claims.quote: Here we get a thumbnail sketch of a campaign setting

claims.claim: Howard contrasts OD&D's Sample Level, a collection of examples, with Holmes presenting his dungeon as part of a coherent adventure.
claims.source: Zach Howard (Zenopus Archives), 'Part 46', 2015
claims.quote: presents his dungeon ideas as part of a coherent adventure

claims.claim: TSR's published Basic Set changed Holmes's manuscript phrase 'one or more assistants' to 'one or more men-at-arms'.
claims.source: Zach Howard (Zenopus Archives), 'Part 46', 2015
claims.quote: changes "one or more assistants" to "one or more men-at-arms"

claims.claim: TSR moved a sentence of Holmes's introduction to the end of its paragraph so it sat immediately before the room descriptions.
claims.source: Zach Howard (Zenopus Archives), 'Part 46', 2015
claims.quote: it places it right before the room descriptions

claims.claim: Howard reports that TSR made only minor changes to Holmes's sample dungeon between manuscript and published rulebook.
claims.source: Zach Howard (Zenopus Archives), 'Part 46', 2015
claims.quote: only minor changes by TSR in the published version

claims.claim: Delta dates the first boxed text in a Gygax adventure to the 1982 published Lost Caverns of Tsojcanth.
claims.source: Delta (Daniel R. Collins), 'Early Evolution of Encounter Text', Delta's D&D Hotspot, 2021
claims.quote: And hey, there's boxed text for the first time!
claims.page: section '1982 - Lost Caverns of Tsojcanth Publication'

claims.claim: In the 1982 Lost Caverns of Tsojcanth the dungeon areas carry boxed text while the wilderness areas do not.
claims.source: Delta (Daniel R. Collins), 'Early Evolution of Encounter Text', 2021
claims.quote: while the dungeon areas use boxed text, the wilderness does not
claims.page: section '1982 - Lost Caverns of Tsojcanth Publication'

claims.claim: Gygax's 1974 Castle Greyhawk notes gave a single curt bullet-line per encounter area.
claims.source: Delta (Daniel R. Collins), 'Early Evolution of Encounter Text', 2021
claims.quote: only a single curt bullet-line per encounter area

claims.claim: Gygax's 1976 Lost Caverns of Tsojconth tournament document moved from bullet points to full English sentences describing each area.
claims.source: Delta (Daniel R. Collins), 'Early Evolution of Encounter Text', 2021
claims.quote: here we at least get full English sentences describing each area
claims.page: section '1976 - Lost Caverns of Tsojconth Tournament'

claims.claim: In the 1978 Steading of the Hill Giant Chief the area paragraphs tend to lead with sense-descriptions.
claims.source: Delta (Daniel R. Collins), 'Early Evolution of Encounter Text', 2021
claims.quote: the paragraphs tend to lead with those sense-descriptions
claims.page: section '1978 - Steading of the Hill Giant Chief'

claims.claim: Expedition to the Barrier Peaks devotes almost 500 words to the Ship Commander's Quarters, an area with no monsters.
claims.source: Delta (Daniel R. Collins), 'Early Evolution of Encounter Text', 2021
claims.quote: almost 500 words total for the one area
claims.page: section '1980 - Expedition to the Barrier Peaks'

claims.claim: Isle of the Ape opens with a boxed speech by Tenser of some 1,600 words to be read verbatim.
claims.source: Delta (Daniel R. Collins), 'Early Evolution of Encounter Text', 2021
claims.quote: 2 full pages of text to be read verbatim
claims.page: section '1984 (c.) - Dungeonland & Temple of Elemental Evil'

claims.claim: The Temple of Elemental Evil's introductory boxed text runs about 1,300 words, more than a full page.
claims.source: Delta (Daniel R. Collins), 'Early Evolution of Encounter Text', 2021
claims.quote: introductory boxed text section that runs more than a full page
claims.page: section '1984 (c.) - Dungeonland & Temple of Elemental Evil'

claims.claim: Delta counts 1,200 words of content text for room 404 of the Temple of Elemental Evil, a 20 by 30 foot room.
claims.source: Delta (Daniel R. Collins), 'Early Evolution of Encounter Text', 2021
claims.quote: room 404 is ironically a 20'×30' room with 1,200 words
claims.page: section '1984 (c.) - Dungeonland & Temple of Elemental Evil'

claims.claim: The Temple of Elemental Evil tends to open an encounter with non-boxed information for the DM before the boxed description.
claims.source: Delta (Daniel R. Collins), 'Early Evolution of Encounter Text', 2021
claims.quote: start with some non-boxed info to the DM, and then
claims.page: section '1984 (c.) - Dungeonland & Temple of Elemental Evil'

claims.claim: Delta locates in the 1982 Tsojcanth the moment monster stat blocks grew too big to sit inside the paragraph text.
claims.source: Delta (Daniel R. Collins), 'Early Evolution of Encounter Text', 2021
claims.quote: monster stat blocks grew too big to comfortably fit within the paragraph
claims.page: section '1982 - Lost Caverns of Tsojcanth Publication'

claims.claim: Delta says boxing his own sensory lead-in would imply reading it verbatim, which he calls a bad idea for a volatile situation.
claims.source: Delta (Daniel R. Collins), comment reply on 'Early Evolution of Encounter Text', 2021
claims.quote: that seems to imply the need to read it verbatim

claims.claim: A reader argues boxed text is linear and assumes the characters approach a room from one specific direction.
claims.source: Warren D., reader comment on Delta's D&D Hotspot, 2021
claims.quote: because it is linear, it often assumes PCs are approaching the room

claims.claim: A reader praises Old-School Essentials room descriptions that bold the important object and put details in parentheses.
claims.source: Warren D., reader comment on Delta's D&D Hotspot, 2021
claims.quote: Room descriptions have important object in bold with parenthesis containing details

claims.claim: In the 1979 Lost Tamoachan the initial area descriptions are set as quoted and indented passages rather than boxed text.
claims.source: Delta (Daniel R. Collins), 'Tip-Offs in Tamoachan', Delta's D&D Hotspot, 2017
claims.quote: not exactly in boxed text, but in specially quoted and indented

claims.claim: Bruce Cordell wrote that the 4e tactical format makes a compelling adventure narrative difficult to generate.
claims.source: Bruce Cordell, Design & Development column (2011), quoted by Mike Bridges, Greyhawkery
claims.quote: The tactical format makes it difficult to generate a compelling adventure narrative
claims.routeHint: direct fetch of the blog quoting the column

claims.claim: Cordell wrote that the tactical format leaves too little space for notes on exploration, lore or character story.
claims.source: Bruce Cordell, Design & Development column (2011), quoted by Mike Bridges, Greyhawkery
claims.quote: adventures tend to be fairly Spartan affairs, because too little space
claims.routeHint: direct fetch of the blog quoting the column

claims.claim: Cordell reports reviewing 1st Edition adventures including Tomb of Horrors for models of adventure format.
claims.source: Bruce Cordell, Design & Development column (2011), quoted by Mike Bridges, Greyhawkery
claims.quote: 1st Edition adventures I looked at included Tomb of Horrors
claims.routeHint: direct fetch of the blog quoting the column

claims.claim: Bill Slavicsek defines a Dungeon Delve as a compact series of encounters appropriate for a specific level of play.
claims.source: Bill Slavicsek, introduction to Dungeon Delve (2009), quoted by Justin Alexander, The Alexandrian
claims.quote: a compact series of encounters appropriate for a specific level of play
claims.routeHint: direct fetch of the blog quoting the book

claims.claim: In 4th Edition adventures, locations with no encounter are compressed into single paragraphs with minimal description.
claims.source: Welcome to the Deathtrap (OSR blog), 'Designing Layout and Information in Adventures', 2021
claims.quote: compressed into single paragraphs with minimal effort spent on description
claims.page: section 'The Evolution of Dungeons & Dragons' Information Design'

claims.claim: The blogger describes 5th Edition's Candlekeep Mysteries as a wall of text with a boxed description.
claims.source: Welcome to the Deathtrap (OSR blog), 2021
claims.quote: it is a wall of text with a boxed description
claims.page: section 'The Evolution of Dungeons & Dragons' Information Design'

claims.claim: 5th Edition still signposts traps and treasure with bold italics at the start of the appropriate paragraph.
claims.source: Welcome to the Deathtrap (OSR blog), 2021
claims.quote: They still signpost traps and treasure with bold italics
claims.page: section 'The Evolution of Dungeons & Dragons' Information Design'

claims.claim: 3rd Edition signposted monsters, treasure, traps and tactics using indentation and icons in a specific order.
claims.source: Welcome to the Deathtrap (OSR blog), 2021
claims.quote: clearly signposted monsters, treasure, traps, and tactics using indentation and icons
claims.page: section 'The Evolution of Dungeons & Dragons' Information Design'

claims.claim: The Dark of Hot Springs Island replaces long box text with a handful of adjectives for the GM to improvise from.
claims.source: Welcome to the Deathtrap (OSR blog), 2021
claims.quote: rather than give a long box text, Hot Springs Island provides

claims.claim: Appelcline calls the Village of Hommlet Greyhawk's first described locale that was not just a dungeon or adventuring point.
claims.source: Shannon Appelcline, 'Designers & Dragons: The Column #24', RPGnet, 2013
claims.quote: first described locale that wasn't just some dungeon or adventuring point

claims.claim: Appelcline says the TSR UK Saltmarsh adventures differ markedly from the staid dungeon crawls US authors were then writing.
claims.source: Shannon Appelcline, 'Designers & Dragons: The Column #24', RPGnet, 2013
claims.quote: how much they differ from the staid dungeon crawls then being

claims.claim: Merwin reports being taught that a short story must hook the reader in the first half-page or go unfinished.
claims.source: Shawn Merwin, 'Let's Design an Adventure: Adventure Hooks and Opening Scenes', D&D Beyond, 2019
claims.quote: unless you hook the reader in the first half-page
claims.page: section 'You May Ask Yourself, How Did I Get Here?'

claims.claim: Merwin says fiction's razor-edge audience-grabbing may not be necessary in adventure writing.
claims.source: Shawn Merwin, 'Let's Design an Adventure: Adventure Hooks and Opening Scenes', D&D Beyond, 2019
claims.quote: might not be necessary in adventure writing
claims.page: section 'You May Ask Yourself, How Did I Get Here?'

claims.claim: Merwin defines the opening scene as the answer to 'where am I' and the hook as the answer to 'why am I here'.
claims.source: Shawn Merwin, 'Let's Design an Adventure: Adventure Hooks and Opening Scenes', D&D Beyond, 2019
claims.quote: The “where” is the opening scene, and the “why” is the adventure hook
claims.page: section 'You May Ask Yourself, How Did I Get Here?'

claims.claim: Merwin judges the way The Village of Hommlet hands over its hook and opening not very exciting or particularly nutritious.
claims.source: Shawn Merwin, 'Let's Design an Adventure: Adventure Hooks and Opening Scenes', D&D Beyond, 2019
claims.quote: It’s not very exciting or particularly nutritious
claims.page: section 'You May Ask Yourself, How Did I Get Here?'

claims.claim: Merwin says an encounter's opening information is probably delivered in the form of boxed text.
claims.source: Shawn Merwin, 'Let's Design an Adventure: Encounter Basics', D&D Beyond, 2019
claims.quote: probably in the form of boxed text or some other vehicle

claims.claim: Merwin locates drama in the dissonance between what characters know entering an encounter and what they learn inside it.
claims.source: Shawn Merwin, 'Let's Design an Adventure: Encounter Basics', D&D Beyond, 2019
claims.quote: There is drama and tension in the dissonance between the information
